paras: Given: x times y, is smaller than zero, and y is smaller than the absolute value of y. Which of the following is necessarily true?

So here we have no numbers at all, just signs. And look at the choices, some of them talk about signs and some about sizes. We'll solve this two ways, first by understanding the givens, and then by plugging in numbers.

Let's take the givens one at a time. When is x times y negative? Only when they have opposite signs, one positive and one negative. Remember, plus times minus is minus. And if both were positive, or both negative, the product would be positive.
But which one is the negative one? We don't know yet. So let's look at the second given.

The second given compares y with its own distance from zero. Let's use that comparison to find which sign y must have. When is a number smaller than its own absolute value? Only when it's negative. If y were positive, they'd just be equal, right? Four is equal to its absolute value. But negative four is smaller than four.
So y is negative, and the signs are opposite. And therefore x is the positive one.
Now the choices. Number one says x is negative. But we just found that x is positive, so number one is out.

Now careful here, because a lot of students think the negative one is also the smaller one. But the givens only tell us signs, nothing about sizes. So we can't know which absolute value is bigger, and numbers two and three don't have to be true.

Number four says the absolute value of x is equal to x. When is a number equal to its absolute value? When it's zero or positive. And x is positive, so this is always true. So number four is our answer.

Now our second method, plugging in numbers. It's a great safety net when you're not sure. I need numbers that obey both givens, and I'll find them by trying. Let's start with y, because the second given has only y in it.

Why do I try a positive y first? Because it's the most natural guess, so let's see if it works. y is three. Is three smaller than the absolute value of three? No, they're equal. And zero is equal to its absolute value too. So y can't be positive, and it can't be zero.
So let's try a negative y, negative three. Is negative three smaller than three? Yes. So negative three works, and now I know y has to be negative.

Now x. What does that mean for x? The first given says x times y is negative. Let's try a negative x too, negative eight. Why eight? So x and y are different numbers, and both stay away from zero and one. Negative three times negative eight is twenty-four. That's positive, so it breaks the first given.
So I adjust, and make x positive, x is eight. Negative three times eight is negative twenty-four, and that's smaller than zero. Now both givens work, so y is negative three and x is eight.

Number one, x is negative? Eight isn't negative, so it's out. Number two says the absolute value of x is smaller. The absolute value of eight is eight, and of negative three it's three. Is eight smaller than three? No, out.

A choice that works for these numbers stays possible for now. We haven't yet shown that it must work for every allowed pair. Number three, negative three over eight, in absolute value, is three eighths. That's less than one, so number three stays. And number four, the absolute value of eight is eight, so it stays too.

Two choices survive. Can I already circle one and move on? I can't, because a necessarily true choice has to work for every pair that fits the givens. So I need a tie-breaker, a new pair that might break one of them. Choice number three is about sizes, so this time I'll make y the bigger one in size, and keep the signs that work. y is negative six, and x is two. Negative six times two is negative twelve, so both givens still hold.
Negative six over two is negative three, and its absolute value is three. That's not less than one, so number three is out. And the absolute value of two is still two. Aaand it's number four, again.
Okay. I'll see you in the next question.

paras: Given: x plus seven, in absolute value, is equal to nine. Which of the following could be the value of x?
So we have an equation with an absolute value, and all the choices are numbers. We'll solve it three ways, two cases, the number line, and plugging in the answers.

The bars surround the whole expression x plus seven. So we'll first find the possible values of that whole expression, then solve for x. Our first method, two cases. Remember, which numbers have an absolute value of nine? Nine, and negative nine. So the inside, x plus seven, is nine, or it's negative nine.

We need to undo the plus seven to isolate x. Subtracting seven from both sides keeps the equality. First case, x plus seven is nine. To get x alone, I take seven off both sides, and x is two. Nine minus seven is two, which gives the value of x in this first case.

In this case the whole inside equals negative nine. We'll still undo the same plus seven. Second case, x plus seven is negative nine. Take seven off again, and x is negative sixteen. Negative nine minus seven is negative sixteen, so that is the second possible x.
Now careful with the choices. Is two there? No. But negative two is there, and that's the trap. It looks like our two, but it's a different number.

Negative sixteen is there, it's number three. And look at the wording, could be. Two values work, two and negative sixteen, but they only offer one of them. So negative sixteen, number three is our answer.

We're going to read the absolute value as a distance between points. The expression inside tells us which fixed point to measure from. Our second method, the number line. Here we read the bars as a distance. Let's start with an easier one. The absolute value of x minus five is seven. Bars around a difference give the distance between two numbers, so this says x is seven steps away from five. Seven steps to the right, five plus seven is twelve. Seven steps to the left, five minus seven is negative two. So x is twelve, or negative two.

Now, what about a plus? x plus seven is x minus negative seven, because taking away negative seven is the same as adding seven. So the absolute value of x plus seven is the distance between x and negative seven. And it's nine, so x is nine steps away from negative seven. Nine steps to the right, negative seven plus nine is two. Nine steps to the left, negative seven minus nine is negative sixteen. Two isn't in the choices, but negative sixteen is, choice number three.

Each choice is a proposed x. Put it inside the original x plus seven, calculate the whole inside, then take its absolute value. And our third method, plugging in the answers. The choices are numbers, so let's just try them. Sixteen plus seven is twenty-three, and twenty-three isn't nine, so no. Negative two plus seven is five, and five isn't nine, so no again.
Negative sixteen plus seven is negative nine, and its absolute value is nine. It works. In the exam you'd circle it and move on.
Okay. I'll see you in the next question.

paras: Given: x plus three, in absolute value, is smaller than seven. Which of the following could be the value of x?

So now the bars are in an inequality, and they're on the small side. What did we say about the small side? It's a closed range. The inside is trapped between seven and negative seven. We'll solve it three ways.

The absolute value must be less than seven. So the whole inside must stay less than seven units from zero, on either side. Our first method, the algebra. The inside is trapped, so I take the seven, and I put negative seven on the other side. So negative seven is smaller than x plus three, which is smaller than seven.
How do I get x alone in the middle? I take three off all three parts. Negative seven minus three is negative ten, and seven minus three is four. So x is between negative ten and four.
Now the choices. Five and eleven are too big, they're above four. Negative twenty-five is too small, it's below negative ten. And three is inside the range. So three, number three is our answer.

The bars around x plus three mean the distance between x and negative three. We're looking for points less than seven units from that fixed point. Our second method, the number line. x plus three is the distance from negative three. So x is less than seven steps away from negative three.

Let's find the two boundary points, then keep the points between them because the distance must be less than seven. Seven steps to the left, negative ten. Seven steps to the right, four. One band in the middle, from negative ten to four. Three is inside it. Five and eleven are past four, and negative twenty-five is way past negative ten, so they're outside. Three, number three.
Our third method, plugging in the answers. Five plus three is eight, not smaller than seven. Negative twenty-five plus three is negative twenty-two, its absolute value is twenty-two. Too big.
Three plus three is six, and six is smaller than seven. It works, so in the exam you circle it and move on.
Okay. I'll see you in the next question.

paras: Given: eight is smaller than x plus one, in absolute value. Which of the following cannot be the value of x?

Let's read it the other way round. Eight is smaller than the bars, so the bars are bigger than eight. They're on the big side. And look at the word cannot. We're looking for the one number that doesn't work. We'll do it three ways.

We need a distance from zero greater than eight. The whole inside can be far enough to the right or far enough to the left. Our first method, two cases. Big side means an open range, one part going to the right and one going to the left. So one option, the inside is bigger than eight. Take one off both sides, and x is bigger than seven.

For the left-hand case, the inside must lie beyond negative eight, farther away from zero. Or, the other option, the inside is smaller than negative eight. Now careful, the sign flips too, because now we're on the negative side. x plus one is smaller than negative eight, so x is smaller than negative nine.
So what does that leave? x can be above seven, or below negative nine, but not in between.

Nine and eleven are bigger than seven, so they can be x. Negative ten is smaller than negative nine, so it can be x too. And two? It's not above seven, and it's not below negative nine. It's stuck in the middle, so x cannot be two. Number two is our answer.

This time the fixed point is negative one. We're looking for all the points more than eight units away from it. Our second method, the number line. x plus one is the distance from negative one. More than eight steps from negative one means past seven on the right, or past negative nine on the left.
Two rays going outward, and a gap in the middle. Two is only three steps from negative one, and three isn't more than eight. So two sits in the gap, and it cannot be x. Number two.
Our third method, plugging in the answers. Nine plus one is ten, and ten is bigger than eight, so nine can be x.
Two plus one is three, and three is not bigger than eight. So two doesn't work. And in a cannot question, the one that doesn't work is the answer. In the exam you'd circle it and move on.
Okay. I'll see you in the next question.

paras: Given: x is smaller than zero. What is ten plus four x over the absolute value of x?

So they're asking what an expression is equal to, and all we know is that x is negative. And what did we say about an expression with a letter? We're allowed to plug in a number. So we'll start with plugging in, and then we'll do the algebra.

Our first method, plugging in numbers. x has to be negative, so I'll take negative two. Why negative two? Before I plug in, I glance at the choices. At negative two they give fourteen, six, two and twelve, all different. So one plug-in will be enough.
Negative six would be a bad pick, by the way. Then minus x is six, and two choices would come out the same.

Use negative two wherever x appears, including inside the bars. We'll calculate the fraction first, then add it to ten. So four times negative two is negative eight. The absolute value of negative two is two. Negative eight over two is negative four, and ten minus four is six.
Which choice gives six at negative two? Only number two. So six, number two is our answer.
Our second method, the algebra. x is negative, so what's its absolute value? To turn a negative number positive, I take minus x. So the absolute value of x is minus x.
Now careful here. A lot of students see minus x and think it's negative. It isn't. x itself is negative, so minus x is positive.

Replacing the absolute value of x with minus x changes the denominator. Let's simplify that fraction before adding ten. So four x over minus x. The x's cancel, and four over minus one is negative four. Ten minus four is six.
And remember this one from earlier in the course. x over its absolute value is always one or minus one. When x is negative, like negative eight over eight, it's minus one.
So the answer doesn't depend on x at all. That's why numbers three and four, with an x in them, can't be right. So six again, number two.
Okay. I'll see you in the next question.

paras: Given: two x minus one, in absolute value, is equal to seven. Which of the following gives all the possible values of x?
So this time there's a number in front of x. And they ask for all the values, so we'll need both cases. Two ways, two cases first, and then plugging in the answers.
Our first method, two cases. Which numbers have an absolute value of seven? Seven and negative seven. So the inside is seven, or the inside is negative seven.

The inside is two x minus one. We'll undo the subtraction first, then undo multiplication by two. First case. Two x minus one is seven. To get x alone, add one, and two x is eight. Divide by two, and x is four.
x is four, so I can already cross out number four. It doesn't have a four in it.
Now careful. A lot of students just flip the sign here and say negative four. But there's a minus one inside the bars, so let's really solve the second case.
Two x minus one is negative seven. Add one, and two x is negative six. Divide by two, and x is negative three.
So four or negative three, number three is our answer. Number one forgets the second case, and number two is the flipped sign.

A choice here gives a set of possible x values. To be the correct set, it must include every value that works and exclude values that don't. Our second method, plugging in the answers. Three of the choices have four in them, so let's test four first. Two times four is eight, minus one, seven. Its absolute value is seven, so four works.
And what does that tell us? Number four is three or negative four, so it leaves out four, a value that works. Number four is out.
Now the other numbers. Negative four. Two times negative four is negative eight, minus one, negative nine. Its absolute value is nine, not seven. So number two is out.

Negative three. Two times negative three is negative six, minus one, negative seven. Its absolute value is seven, so it works too. So number one, four only, misses negative three. It's four or negative three, number three.

So two cases, two answers, and don't assume they're opposites. When there's a number in front of x, or a number added inside, solve the second case all the way. Okay. I'll see you in the next question.

paras: Which of the following has no solution?
So we're looking for the one that no number can satisfy. And before any algebra, look at the right sides. Two of them are negative, and one is zero. That's our hint.
Remember, an absolute value is never negative. It can be zero, it can be positive, but it can never go below zero.

We're looking for a statement with no solution. Finding even one value of x that works is enough to rule a choice out. Number one. The bars are equal to zero. Can that happen? Yes, when the inside is zero. x minus three is zero, so x is three. It has a solution, so it's out.
Number two. The bars are smaller than negative one. But the bars are never negative, so they can never be below negative one. No number works.
Number three looks almost the same, but the sign goes the other way. The bars are bigger than negative one. And that's always true, because the bars are zero or more. Every x works, so it's out.
Number four. The absolute value of x is at most one. Zero works, because zero is at most one. So it has a solution, and it's out.
So x plus two, in absolute value, smaller than negative one has no solution. Number two is our answer.

The direction of the inequality is what decides whether the nonnegative absolute value can satisfy it. Now look at numbers two and three again. The same numbers, and a different sign. One is never true, and the other one is always true.
And it works the same way for equations. Bars equal to a negative number, like bars equal to negative five, have no solution at all.
Is there a second way? Sure, try to find one solution for each choice. Number one, try three. Three minus three is zero, so three works.
Number three, try zero. Zero plus two is two, and two is bigger than negative one, so zero works. Number four, zero again, and zero is at most one. Works.
Number two, whatever x I try, x plus two in bars comes out zero or more. Try zero, it's two. Try negative two, it's zero. It never gets below negative one. So no solution, number two.
So always look at the right side first. A negative number or a zero there is a gift. Okay. I'll see you in the next question.

From three to seven there are five numbers, three, four, five, six, seven, and seven minus three is only four. Both ends count.

Three-digit numbers start at a hundred and stop just below a thousand. Let's find the first and last multiples of fifteen inside that range. Fifteen. paras: Given: c is equal to four a, and a is equal to b over five. a, b and c are positive integers. Which claim is not necessarily true?

So the two givens tell us how a, b and c are related. We're looking for the claim that does not have to be true. That means we need a choice that can fail, even when both givens are satisfied. One example where it fails is enough. We'll solve it two ways, writing everything with a, and then plugging in numbers.

Let's start with one letter, a. The first given says c is four a, which means four times a. a is a whole number, so c is always four times a whole number. That means c is always divisible by four. Choice number one is always true, so it's not what we're looking for. Out.

The second given says a is b over five. Multiply both sides by five, and b is five a. So b is always five times a whole number, which means b always divides by five. Choice number two is always true, so it's out too.

Now let's check a plus b. We already found that b is five a, so replace b with five a. That's a plus five a, which is six a. The sum always divides by six. But does it always divide by twelve, as choice number three claims? Only when a is even. If a is two, a plus b is twelve, and that works. But if a is one, a plus b is six, and six doesn't divide by twelve. So this claim can fail, and choice number three is our answer.

In the exam you'd circle it and move on. Here, let's check the last choice too. It says a plus b plus c divides by ten. Replace b with five a and c with four a. a plus b plus c is a plus five a plus four a, which is ten a. That's always ten times a whole number, so it is always divisible by ten. This claim is true too.

Now let's try plugging in numbers. Our numbers must satisfy both givens and be positive integers. Start with the condition a is b over five. We need that division to give a whole number, so let's choose b is five. Then a is one. Use that same a in the first given: c is four times one, which is four. So our values are a is one, b is five, and c is four.

Let's check the choices with these values. c is four, divisible by four, so the first claim works for this example. b is five, divisible by five, so the second claim works too. Now the third claim: a plus b is one plus five, which is six. Six is not divisible by twelve, so the third claim fails.

So the third claim fails with numbers that satisfy both givens. That's exactly what not necessarily true means: the claim does not work for every allowed set of numbers. One failing example is all we need. Choice number three is our answer. Okay. I'll see you in the next question.

paras: x and y are positive integers. x is divisible by six, and y is divisible by nine. What is the largest number that x plus y is necessarily divisible by?

So x is a multiple of six, and y is a multiple of nine. We add them, and we want the largest number that their sum always divides by, whatever allowed values of x and y we choose. We'll solve it two ways, writing each number as a multiplication, and then plugging in numbers.

Let's start by writing the multiples. x is six k, meaning six times some positive whole number k. And y is nine m, meaning nine times some positive whole number m. We use separate letters because we can choose each multiple independently. Nothing says k and m are equal. They may happen to be equal, but we cannot assume that they are.

We're looking for a number that the sum always divides by, whatever values k and m have. Let's look at the two parts separately. Six k is three times two k. And nine m is three times three m. So both parts are multiples of three, and adding them gives another multiple of three. We can write six k plus nine m as three times the whole bracket, two k plus three m. k and m are whole numbers, so the calculation inside the bracket also gives a whole number. Our sum is always three times a whole number, so it is always divisible by three. Changing k and m changes the number inside the bracket, but it doesn't remove the three multiplying that bracket.

Let's see the same idea with multiples of four and of six. Four k plus six m is two times the whole bracket, two k plus three m, because both four k and six m are multiples of two. So their sum is always divisible by two. But it does not have to divide by four: four plus six is ten, and ten doesn't divide by four. Notice that this is a rule about adding. If we multiplied instead, six k times nine m would be fifty-four k m, because six times nine is fifty-four and k times m is k m.

We know the sum is always divisible by three. Could a bigger number always divide it too? With k and m one, the bracket is five and the sum is three times five, fifteen. With k two and m one, the bracket is seven and the sum is three times seven, twenty-one. Any guaranteed divisor must divide both fifteen and twenty-one. Fifteen is three times five, and twenty-one is three times seven. Their largest common divisor is three. So no bigger number can be guaranteed, and choice number three is our answer.

Now let's try plugging in numbers. Choose x is six and y is nine. Both satisfy their divisibility conditions. Six plus nine is fifteen, and fifteen doesn't divide by eighteen or by nine. So choice numbers one and four are out.

Fifteen does divide by fifteen, so our first example hasn't ruled out that choice. Let's try another allowed pair. x is twelve and y is nine. x still divides by six, and y still divides by nine. Twelve plus nine is twenty-one, and twenty-one doesn't divide by fifteen. So fifteen is out too. Only three is left, and choice number three is our answer.

Now careful, here's the trap in choice number one. Eighteen is divisible by both six and nine, so you might choose eighteen for both x and y. Eighteen plus eighteen is thirty-six, and it divides by eighteen. But that only tells us eighteen works for this particular pair. Nothing says x and y must be equal, and we already found an allowed pair where the sum does not divide by eighteen. So eighteen is not guaranteed. Okay. I'll see you in the next question.

paras: When x is divided by eight, the remainder is four. Yuval claims: two x is necessarily divisible by eight. Noga claims: x is necessarily divisible by four. Itay claims: x is necessarily divisible by twelve. Which of the following is correct?

So dividing x by eight leaves four. Each person says something about what x divides by. Which claims always work? We'll solve it three ways, thinking about the remainder, writing x with a letter, and then plugging in numbers.

Let's start with the meaning of the remainder. x is made of complete groups of eight, with four left over. If eight is divisible by the new divisor, those complete groups also divide without a remainder. So then we only need to check the four left over.

Let's check Yuval's claim that two x divides by eight. Doubling x doubles both its complete groups of eight and the four left over. The doubled groups still divide by eight. And the leftover part becomes two times four, which is eight. That divides by eight too, so two x always divides by eight. Yuval is right.

Now let's check Noga's claim that x divides by four. Each complete group of eight contains two complete groups of four. So those groups leave no remainder when divided by four. The leftover four also divides by four: four over four is one, with no remainder. Both parts divide by four, so x always divides by four. Noga is right.

Now let's check Itay's claim that x divides by twelve. Eight does not divide by twelve, so our complete groups of eight do not necessarily divide by twelve. The original remainder is not enough to guarantee this claim. For example, x is four. Four divided by eight leaves four, as required, but four doesn't divide by twelve. This allowed value makes Itay's claim fail, so Itay is wrong.
Yuval and Noga are right, and only Itay is wrong. So choice number two is our answer.

paras: Before you practice, let's review the main rules for divisibility and remainders.

For each divisor, check the part of the number that decides divisibility. For two, five and ten, look at the last digit. For three and nine, add the digits and check that sum. For four, check the number formed by the last two digits. For eight, check the number formed by the last three digits.

For eleven, alternate subtraction and addition across the digits. For nine hundred thirteen, calculate nine minus one plus three, which is eleven. Eleven divides by eleven, so the original number does too.

For a larger divisor, split it into two numbers that multiply to make it. No number greater than one should divide both of them. For thirty-six, use four times nine. Check divisibility by both four and nine. Checking six twice only repeats the same condition, so six times six is not the right split for this test.

When we divide, we get complete groups and sometimes a remainder. The original number is the divisor times the number of complete groups, plus the remainder. The remainder must be smaller than the divisor. So the biggest remainder is the divisor minus one. If the number is smaller than the divisor, we cannot make even one complete group. Five divided by eight leaves five, not three.

When dividing by three or nine, the original number and its digit sum have the same remainder. For four thousand eight hundred twenty-six, the digit sum is twenty. Twenty divided by nine leaves two, so the original number also leaves two when divided by nine.

For addition, subtraction and multiplication, work with the remainders instead of the whole numbers. Say a leaves five and b leaves seven when divided by eight. For a plus b, five plus seven is twelve. Twelve leaves four when divided by eight, so the sum leaves four. For a times b, five times seven is thirty-five. Thirty-five leaves three, so the product leaves three. For a minus b, five minus seven is negative two. A remainder cannot be negative, so add eight. Negative two plus eight is six, which is the remainder. The divisor stays eight in all three checks.
Subtract the remainder from the original number. The part left divides exactly, with no remainder.

If we change the number we're dividing by, can we use the remainder we already know? Yes, if the old divisor divides by the new one. Suppose a number leaves eleven when divided by twelve. Twelve divides by four, so all the complete twelves divide by four too. We only need to check the eleven left over. Eleven leaves three when divided by four, so the original number leaves three too. But ten does not divide by four. So knowing a remainder for ten does not tell us the remainder for four.

For a fraction of another fraction, with one on top of each, multiply the bottom numbers. One fifth of one third is one over fifteen, because five times three is fifteen. For other fractions, simplify first and check that each group is a whole number. To count multiples in a range, find the first and last multipliers. Subtract the first multiplier from the last, then add one because both ends count.

For integers in a row, these rules are about their product. The product of two numbers in a row always divides by two. The product of three numbers in a row always divides by six. And a cubed minus a can be written as a minus one, times a, times a plus one, which are three numbers in a row.

If a number must divide by something, write it as that divisor times a whole number. Then we can see what it always divides by. When plugging in, choose values that fit every given. Let's count the twos. For division by eight to give an integer, the whole top must divide by eight. We need three twos in its multiplication. b is even, so write b as two times an integer k.
Choice number one includes b cubed. b is two k, so its cube is eight k cubed. That gives a whole eight on top. Dividing by the eight on the bottom leaves an integer, so this choice is out.

The two a squared parts cancel too, leaving two b squared. b is two k, so b squared is four k squared. Two times that is eight k squared. That divides by eight, so this choice is out.

paras: Before you practice, let's review the main rules: positive and negative numbers, numbers in a row, and even and odd numbers.

When we multiply or divide two numbers, the same signs give a positive result. Different signs give a negative result. Negative two times negative five is ten. Negative two times five is negative ten. When we multiply many numbers, count how many are negative to find the result's sign.

When we add a positive number and a negative number, compare their sizes without the signs. The larger size decides the result's sign. Negative nine plus four is negative five. Also, a larger number minus a smaller number gives a positive result, even if both are negative. Negative three minus negative eight is five.
An even power gives a result that is positive or zero. An odd power keeps the number's sign. And minus x means the opposite of x, so it is positive when x is negative.
For numbers in a row, use one letter for the middle and write the other numbers around it. Even numbers in a row, or odd numbers in a row, have a gap of two.

For equally spaced numbers, the middle is their average. To find their sum, multiply that middle value by how many numbers there are. From sixteen to twenty, there are five numbers. The middle is eighteen, so their sum is five times eighteen, which is ninety.
From integer a to integer b, including both ends, there are b minus a plus one integers. If a and b are neighboring integers, b squared minus a squared equals a plus b.
To check whether a sum is even or odd, count its odd numbers. The even numbers do not change the result's type. For a product, one even number is enough to make the whole product even.

An odd integer divided by a nonzero even integer cannot give an integer. Positive whole-number powers keep a number even or odd. So when that is all we need to check, we can check the numbers without those powers.

When plugging in numbers, start with one easy example that fits every given. We do not need to know in advance how many choices it will rule out. Check the choices straight away, and cross out each one that fails. If only one choice remains, stop. If several remain, choose another easy example with a different useful feature, and explain why that feature may help. Do not do a fixed number of tests just because there is division. And if examples cannot separate overlapping descriptions, use the rule to decide which description is most precise.

Now the rules for products of numbers in a row. Multiply two integers in a row, and their product is divisible by two. For three in a row, the product is divisible by six. For four in a row, it is divisible by twenty-four. And the product of two even numbers in a row is divisible by eight.

To check division by a power of two, count how many twos are in the multiplication. For a divisor that must always work, the smallest allowed example can rule out choices immediately. If several divisors still fit, try another allowed example that does not have one of those extra factors. Stop once only one choice remains. That's it. paras: Given: one is smaller than p, which is smaller than q, which is smaller than r, which is smaller than s. Which of the following statements is not correct?
So p, q, r and s are all greater than one, in that order. We need the statement that is not correct. We'll solve it two ways, comparing the numbers we multiply, and then plugging in numbers.

Let's start by comparing products. All our numbers are positive. Match the larger number in one product with the larger number in the other, and do the same with the smaller numbers. If both numbers in one product are larger, that product is larger too. For example, compare two times three with four times five. Four is larger than two, and five is larger than three. So four times five is larger.

Choice number one compares p times q with r squared. r squared means r times r. r is larger than p, and r is larger than q. So r times r is larger than p times q. The statement is correct, so this choice is out.

Choice number two compares q with s times p. s is already larger than q. Multiplying s by p makes it even larger, because p is greater than one. So q is smaller than s times p. This statement is correct too, so it's out.

Choice number three compares r times p with q. r is already larger than q, and multiplying by p makes r larger still. So r times p is larger than q. But the choice says it is smaller. That's the incorrect statement, so choice number three is our answer.
Now let's try plugging in. Choose numbers that are all greater than one and in the given order: p is two, q is three, r is four, and s is five.

Choice number one: two times three is six, and four squared is sixteen. Six is smaller than sixteen, so the statement works. Choice number two: five times two is ten, and three is smaller than ten. That statement works too. Choice number three: four times two is eight, but eight is not smaller than three. That statement fails. So choice number three is our answer. Okay. I'll see you in the next question.

4 > 2, and 5 > 3. So 4 × 5 is larger.

So r × r > p × q. The statement is correct, so this choice is out.

Choice number 2 compares q with s × p. s is already larger than q.
Multiplying s by p makes it even larger, because p > 1. So q < s × p.
This statement is correct too, so it's out.

Choice number 3 compares r × p with q. r is already larger than q, and multiplying by p makes r larger still.
So r × p > q. But the choice says it is smaller. That's the incorrect statement, so choice number 3 is our answer.

Now let's try plugging in.
Choose numbers that are all greater than 1 and in the given order: p = 2, q = 3, r = 4, and s = 5.

Choice number 1: 2 × 3 = 6, and 4² = 16. 6 < 16, so the statement works.
Choice number 2: 5 × 2 = 10, and 3 < 10. That statement works too.

So choice number 3 is our answer. Okay. I'll see you in the next question.

paras: Welcome back. Last time we saw the four ranges on the number line and what multiplication and division do in each one. Now let's look at powers. This method may feel new at first, but with practice it can help you compare answers quickly.

Draw the number line and mark its four ranges: below negative one, between negative one and zero, between zero and one, and above one. We'll call the two middle ranges negative fractions and positive fractions.

In the powers and roots topics, we learned how to calculate these expressions. Here we want to know which result is larger, without calculating every result. If the question uses letters, we may not know the original number.

First find the original number's range. Then check whether each result is positive or negative. An even power of a negative number is positive, so it is larger than every negative result. When results have the same sign, the arrows will help us compare them.
We keep the original number the same and compare different powers of it. Put an arrow in each range. It shows which way the result moves when we increase the power.
Above one, the arrow points right. Between zero and one, it points left.

For a negative number, use the arrow only for powers that leave the result negative. Even powers make it positive, so check them separately. Between negative one and zero, the arrow points right. Below negative one, it points left. These negative-side arrows apply to odd powers.
Moving right means the result is larger. Moving left means it is smaller. As we increase the power, we move farther in the arrow's direction.

Above one, the arrow points right. A larger power gives a larger result. Start with two: two squared is four, and two cubed is eight. With three, the results are three, nine and twenty-seven. They get larger as the power increases.

A square root is a power of one half. That is smaller than the power of one in x itself. So for x above one, the square root is smaller than x, but still greater than one. The square root of four is two, and the square root of nine is three. At exactly one, every result is one. So pay attention to the ends of each range.

Between zero and one, the arrow points left. A larger power gives a smaller result. One half squared is one quarter, smaller than one half. One third squared is one ninth, and one third cubed is one twenty-seventh.

Now three sevenths. Its square is nine forty-ninths. Which is larger, three sevenths or its square? We do not need to calculate. Squaring increases the power from one to two. The arrow points left, so the square is smaller.

A square root lowers the power from one to one half, so we move against the arrow. Between zero and one, that makes the result larger. The square root of one ninth is one third. In an exam question we may have letters instead of numbers. The arrows let us compare the results even then.

Between negative one and zero, the arrow points right for odd powers. Remember, a negative number closer to zero is larger. Negative one half cubed is negative one eighth. That is closer to zero, to the right of negative one half. Negative one third cubed is negative one twenty-seventh, also to the right of the original number.

Why not even powers? They make the negative number positive, so the result moves across zero to the other side. Every positive number is larger than every negative number. Negative one half squared is positive one quarter.

Which powers keep the result negative? Odd powers like three and five, and negative odd powers like negative one and negative three. Odd roots do too. A cube root is a power of one third, and a fifth root is a power of one fifth. We can use the same arrow to compare these results.

Below negative one, the arrow points left for odd powers. The result gets larger in size, but stays negative. So its value on the number line is smaller. Negative two cubed is negative eight. Negative three cubed is negative twenty-seven. Both results are to the left of the original numbers.
Even powers make these numbers positive too. Check those results separately, before using the negative-side arrow.
For a question comparing powers, use three steps. First check results that change sides. A negative number raised to an even power becomes positive.
Second, write roots as powers, so we can compare the powers directly. The fifth root of x is x to the power of one fifth.

Third, find the number's range, draw its arrow, and compare the powers. Keep negative powers as they are when using this method. Negative one is smaller than the positive powers, so we can place it in the comparison too.
Sometimes we are given the order of the results and need to find the original number's range. For example, x is smaller than x to the fifth, and x to the fifth is smaller than x to the fourth.

Check the two comparisons separately. First, x is smaller than x to the fifth. We increased the power from one to five, and the result got larger. That fits a right-pointing arrow: above one, or between negative one and zero. It does not fit the other two ranges, so they are out.

Now x to the fifth is smaller than x to the fourth. Above one, the fifth power would be larger than the fourth, not smaller. So that range is out too. Only the range between negative one and zero is left.

In that range, x to the fifth is negative. x to the fourth is positive because the power is even. So the fourth power is larger, just as the question says. Questions like this come up less often, but the range rules still help. You can also plug in numbers, though that takes more calculation. Okay. I'll see you in the next video.

That means a larger power gives a larger result. The largest power is seven, so y to the seventh must be last in the list, at the largest end. Choice number one ends with y to the negative seven, and choice number two ends with y itself. Neither can be correct, so both are out.

paras: Before you practice, let's review the ranges, the powers, and how to read the number line.
Start with four ranges: below negative one, between negative one and zero, between zero and one, and above one. The operation rules work the same way for every number within each range.

Pay attention to negative one, zero and one, which separate the ranges. If we only know that x is positive, it could be between zero and one, equal to one, or greater than one. On the negative side, remember that a number farther from zero is smaller, not larger.

For a positive number, multiplying by a number greater than one makes it larger. Dividing by a positive fraction smaller than one also makes it larger. Twelve divided by one third is thirty-six. Dividing by a number greater than one, or multiplying by a positive fraction smaller than one, makes it smaller. Twelve times one third is four.

For a negative number, these operations still move it away from zero or towards zero. But farther from zero means smaller, and closer to zero means larger. Multiplying by a negative number changes sides and reverses the order. Four is smaller than nine, but negative four is larger than negative nine.

If one number is in a higher range than another, taking the same positive power or root keeps that order. Six fifths is above one, and two thirds is between zero and one. So the cube root of six fifths is larger than the cube root of two thirds, without calculating either. For negative numbers, use this rule only with odd powers and odd roots.

When the same operation keeps the order, we can compare the original numbers instead of calculating both results. For positive numbers, the same positive power or root keeps the order. And for products of positive numbers, compare the numbers we multiply in pairs. If both numbers in one product are larger than their matches in the other, that product is larger.

Some powers move the result into another range, so check them first. The whole number negative three, squared, is positive nine. But a minus sign outside the square gives minus three squared, which is negative nine. The brackets matter. A negative power means take the reciprocal. Two thirds to the negative two is three halves squared, so the result is above one.

The arrows show what happens as we increase the power. Above one, the arrow points right. Between zero and one, left. Between negative one and zero, right. Below negative one, left. For negative numbers, use these arrows only for powers that keep the result negative. Right means larger, and left means smaller.

Use three steps: check results that change sign, write roots as powers, then use the arrows. With the arrows, keep negative powers as they are. If we are given the results' order and need the original range, check which range's arrow fits that order. Or test numbers from the ranges.
One over x, the reciprocal, keeps the sign of nonzero x. For numbers with the same sign, taking reciprocals reverses their order. Three is smaller than five, but one third is larger than one fifth.

When plugging in, start with an easy number in the allowed range. Two, one half, negative one half and negative two are useful options for different ranges, not a list we must always test. Check the answer choices after the first example. Try another only if more than one choice remains, and choose a different useful feature. If there is a root, use an easy root: one ninth for a square root, or negative one eighth for a cube root. Replace only the letters. For a statement that must be true, one allowed example where it fails is enough to rule it out. Values near the ends of the ranges can help. For a number-line picture, first write each letter's range. If it is not drawn to scale, trust the order, not the distances.

To find a distance on the number line, subtract the smaller number from the larger. To find a new point, we also need where we start and which way we move. For one third of the way, take one third of the distance and move that far from the starting point. For the midpoint, find the average of the two ends. That's it. Now go practice, and I'll see you in the next video.

paras: A, B, C and D represent digits. Given: B A, plus D A, is equal to C C A. B plus C plus D is equal to what?
B A and D A are two-digit numbers. C C A is the three-digit result of adding them. Each letter stands for one digit in those numbers. We'll use our four steps to solve the addition.
Step one, write the addition vertically, with the ones digits in one column and the tens digits in the next. Now we can check each column.

Step two, the ones column. We add A plus A, and the result must end in A again. So adding another A does not change the last digit. A is a single digit, and nothing carries into the ones column. The only digit we can add without changing that last digit is zero. Five plus zero ends in five, and eight plus zero ends in eight. So A is zero.
Step three, the leftmost digit. We added two two-digit numbers and got a three-digit number. That new hundreds digit can only be one. Here that digit is C, so C is one.

Why can it only be one? Even ninety-nine plus ninety-nine is just a hundred ninety-eight, below two hundred. And ninety plus ninety is a hundred eighty. So when two two-digit numbers give a three-digit sum, its hundreds digit is one. This rule is for adding two numbers. Adding three or four numbers can give a larger first digit.

Now check the tens column. A is zero, so zero plus zero carries nothing into this column. C is one, so the result has one in both its tens and hundreds places. That means B plus D is eleven. B and D could be three and eight, or four and seven. We do not need to find them separately.
The question asks for B plus C plus D. B plus D is eleven, and C is one. Add them to get twelve. Choice number four is our answer.
We can check the examples: thirty plus eighty is a hundred ten. Forty plus seventy is a hundred ten too. Both fit the addition. Okay. I'll see you in the next question.

paras: Before you practice, let's review what the letters mean, the four steps, and the useful number facts.
A bar above the letters means they are digits of one number. The two-digit number A B means ten A plus B, not A times B. The three-digit number A B C means a hundred A plus ten B plus C.
Use the same digit every time the same letter appears. A leading digit cannot be zero. Different letters do not have to be different digits unless the question says they are different.

Use four steps: write the calculation vertically, check the ones column, check the leading digit and the size, then try numbers if needed. If the question asks for one letter, try the answer choices for that letter.

For a puzzle written in words, write each number using its digits. A two-digit number is ten A plus B. For example, if ten A plus B equals three times the whole bracket, A plus B, open the bracket and collect the A parts and B parts. We get seven A equals two B. The digits that fit give the number twenty-seven.

If X plus Y ends in X in the ones column, Y must be zero. Nothing carries into that column. In another column, check the carry too. Without an incoming carry, the added digit is zero. With a carried one, it is nine, because nine plus that one makes ten and keeps the last digit unchanged.

When we add two numbers with the same number of digits, and the sum has an extra digit, its new leading digit is one. Seventy-six plus fifty-eight is a hundred thirty-four. This rule is for adding two numbers, not three or more.

The special digits are zero, one, five and six. Squaring one of these keeps the same last digit. Fifteen times fifteen is two hundred twenty-five, still ending in five. Sixteen times sixteen is two hundred fifty-six, still ending in six.
For subtraction, read the equality as addition. For division, read it as multiplication. That can make the digit columns easier to check.

For reversal questions, keep the same digits and reverse their positions. A two-digit number plus its reversal is divisible by eleven. Their difference is divisible by nine. For three-digit numbers, the difference is divisible by ninety-nine.
The repeated-digit number A A A is a hundred eleven times A. So it is divisible by three and thirty-seven. Four hundred forty-four is thirty-seven times twelve.

For the largest number with a given digit sum, put as much as possible in the left-hand places. For the smallest, keep the left-hand digits as small as possible, while leaving room for the remaining sum on the right. The first digit cannot be zero, and each digit is at most nine.
